steps.label: KP07 The full gradient scans all the data at every step
The cost of the full gradient · 1/7
steps.speakerNotes: The goal is to minimize the average loss over n samples. Differentiation is linear, so the full gradient is the average of per-sample gradients.

steps.label: The cost of the full gradient · 1/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The price is that every update needs a forward and backward pass over all n samples.

steps.label: The cost of the full gradient · 1/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: With n equal a million, one step scans a million samples.

steps.label: The cost of the full gradient · 1/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: With n in the billions one step takes hours and training cannot move.

steps.label: The cost of the full gradient · 1/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: n in the billions one step takes hours training cannot move

steps.label: The cost of the full gradient · 1/7 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: Rather than one exact gradient, take many steps with a cheap stand-in.

steps.label: The idea of SGD · 2/7
steps.speakerNotes: The idea is plain: each step draws one sample at random and uses its gradient as a stand-in for the full gradient.

steps.label: The idea of SGD · 2/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Each step runs a forward and backward pass on one sample only, cost O(1) independent of n.

steps.label: The idea of SGD · 2/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The stand-in is acceptable because it is unbiased: the expected single-sample gradient equals the full gradient.

steps.label: The idea of SGD · 2/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: unbiased \mathbb{E}_i[\nabla f_i(w)]=\nabla F(w)

steps.label: The idea of SGD · 2/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: That is, the expected direction is the true full gradient. In the time of one full gradient, single-sample updates can take thousands of steps.

steps.label: Checking unbiasedness · 3/7
steps.speakerNotes: Four samples, each loss one half of w minus a squared, with a equal 2, 4, 6, 8. At w equal 0 the four gradients are minus 2, minus 4, minus 6, minus 8.

steps.label: Checking unbiasedness · 3/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Their average is minus 5.

steps.label: Checking unbiasedness · 3/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The full gradient is w minus 5, which at 0 is minus 5.

steps.label: Checking unbiasedness · 3/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The average equals the full gradient: that is unbiasedness.

steps.label: Checking unbiasedness · 3/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: average = full gradient: unbiased the single-sample gradients differ but average to the full gradient

steps.label: Noise · 4/7
steps.speakerNotes: At the minimum, w equal 5, the full gradient is zero but the four single-sample gradients are 3, 1, minus 1, minus 3, none zero.

steps.label: Noise · 4/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The single-sample variance is 5, the standard deviation 2.236.

steps.label: Noise · 4/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: If sample one is drawn with learning rate 0.2, w becomes 4.4: already at the minimum yet pushed away in one step.

steps.label: Noise · 4/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: A single-sample gradient is the true gradient plus zero-mean noise: right on average, but each step carries a random error.

steps.label: Noise · 4/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: \nabla f_i=\nabla F+\xi_i, \mathbb{E}[\xi_i]=0: right on average, with a random error every step the expected direction is right; a single step can be wrong

steps.label: The size of the swing · 5/7
steps.speakerNotes: Let the error be w minus 5; the update is 1 minus eta times the error plus eta times zero-mean noise. The steady-state standard deviation is sigma times the square root of eta over 2 minus eta.

steps.label: The size of the swing · 5/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Learning rate 0.05 swings about 0.34, 0.2 about 0.745, 0.5 about 1.29.

steps.label: The size of the swing · 5/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A smaller rate swings less but converges slower.

steps.label: The size of the swing · 5/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: a smaller rate swings less but converges slower (KP02's “too small”) \eta=0.2: 2.236\cdot\sqrt{0.2/1.8}=0.745

steps.label: The trade-offs · 6/7
steps.speakerNotes: How to make SGD truly settle? Decay the step so the influence of noise shrinks.

steps.label: The trade-offs · 6/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With learning rate 1 over k plus 1, each update gives exactly the sample average of all a drawn so far.

steps.label: The trade-offs · 6/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The trade-off in one phrase: cheap but noisy. Cost per step falls from n to 1; the gradient is unbiased but noisy.

steps.label: The trade-offs · 6/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Not every step descends; it keeps swinging near the minimum unless the step decays.

steps.label: The trade-offs · 6/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: The source says noise helps escape saddles and generalizes better; that may hold under some conditions but is not guaranteed, left to KP12.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: “unbiased means every step descends”. the expected direction is right but one step can go wrong

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: “SGD is always faster than full gradient descent”. cheap steps, but more of them

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “fixed-step SGD converges to the minimum”. it only swings around it

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Single-sample noise is still too large. Can we compromise with a small batch per step?
